children.text: Elections in Boulder, in the state of Colorado and across the country have the context of a failed war, policies that enrich the few at the expense of the many, and a general feeling of state and local governments dealing with the effects of an immoral and incompetent federal government run by Republicans.

Nothing epitomizes how the majority of Americans feel about the federal government more than the unlawful attacks on The National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado. That Republicans and the president have acted to greatly harm a world-recognized institution, potentially in the course of
political vengeance
, is appalling.
At the state level, Colorado and states across the country have been working to mitigate the
large cuts enabled by Republicans

’ 2025 HR1 (One Big Beautiful Bill). While it’s hard to be optimistic, Democratic measures on the ballot can begin to tackle the problem, as long as we also defeat the 10+ right-wing measures put onto the ballot by
Advance Colorado
and other dark-money funded groups.

In Boulder, we have a significant number of wins from the previous several years — making consistent progress on Boulder’s goals around housing, transportation, climate, and social equity. The City of Boulder also faces difficult budget and funding challenges which I also hope to see carried out by passing a number of council-initiated ballot measures.

My hope for 2026 is that Colorado and Boulder can keep their heads down, doing the critical work that needs to be done. At the same, we need people and elected leaders that are willing to fight back at the federal government illegality and break the Republican strangle-hold on the United States. It is the imperative.
About Boulder Colorado Voter Guide and Disclosures

In full disclosure, I am very involved in local and statewide politics. I serve on leadership for organizations that endorse and support candidates: Boulder Progressives and Better Boulder, and am a co-founder of
Colorado Community Research

, a Boulder-based polling and political consulting company. Since 2021, I’ve been more involved than ever — working to end discriminatory occupancy limits statewide, running a campaign to move Boulder’s municipal elections to even years, helping pass the city’s library district ballot measure, proposing and supporting a successful effort to set fair wages for city council members, and helping to pass statewide housing reforms. I’ve interviewed or talked with about a dozen candidates running for city council or school board this year as parts of various endorsement processes.
I’ve written a voter guide for every general election in Boulder for the past ten-plus years. I want to start with a thank you to local journalists: news and opinion writers at the

I'm ranking 1. Aaron Brockett and 2. Taishya Adams

I am voting for Aaron Brockett as my choice for Boulder’s mayor. His work on Boulder City Council since 2015 (plus a previous term on Boulder’s Planning Board) have really shown a depth of knowledge and ability in leading the city, as well as making progress on a number of long-term priorities.

Aaron Brockett and the council have accomplished a massive amount in just the past three years. The work on housing, transportation, climate and sustainability is significant compared to the pace of change in the past few decades. I’ve updated a list of accomplishments included in my voter guide for the 2025 election (which was Boulder’s last off-cycle election before moving to even-year municipal elections):
Updated the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan to significantly expand Boulder’s possible long-term housing supply
Strengthened Boulder’s wildfire hardening and resilience code
Implemented Boulder's mandate that new buildings are all-electric and natural-gas free
Supporting and approving a measure to set future council’s pay based on the median city wage
Supported Colorado’s law to end discriminatory housing occupancy limits statewide in Colorado
Established Boulder’s first citywide minimum wage
Ended city-mandated parking requirements
Expanded housing on transit corridors
Expanded work on the Core Arterial Network to improve transportation
Improved safety for people walking, biking, busing, and driving
Established a transportation maintenance fee (first proposed in the early 2010s) as a permanent funding mechanism to improve maintenance on roads, bike paths, multi-use paths, and sidewalks
Expanded housing options for townhomes, duplexes, and Accessory Dwelling Units
What are the biggest challenges that the next mayor and city council will face?

Again, since it’s only been a year since the last municipal election, I’m going to revisit my list of challenges from 2025 and add new thoughts. Every city council has known challenges and unknown challenges. Here are a few things that the next city council will certainly be grappling with:
Additional focus to allow more Middle Income Housing to be built in Boulder

Boulder continues to make progress here from a zoning and transportation perspective, but likely the city will need to continue implementing both its comprehensive plan and state laws to keep making progress.
Reduced city budget for social services and
Reduced funding for homelessness services (ARPA)
Boulder’s 2026 budget reduced spending on housing and human services by 2.65%, while the
proposed 2027 budget
would reduce funding by an additional 3.11%.

The City of Boulder budget continues to be under increased pressure due to stagnant sales and property tax revenue.

While the city hasn’t seen a significant reduction in federal transportation funding, existing projects are subject to federal matching funds which
may be at risk later this year

Continued demographic shift to older and wealthier populations
Only a year later, but the city (and county) are unlikely to see a change in aging trends anytime soon.
Continued steep drops in school enrollment
The Boulder Valley School District has identified challenges with declining enrollment for five to ten years. Just in the past month, school officials and the

children.text: Boulder’s mayor election uses ranked choice voting. Who else to consider?
I am voting for Aaron Brockett ranked first, but I wanted to write about a few other candidates.
Taishya Adams

I supported Taishya Adams for Boulder City Council in 2023, and think that she has been a solid council person in passing many of the progressive priorities accomplished in the past three years. I have wanted to see more leadership here in working on moving the city forward on the core functions of housing, transportation, and land use. I appreciate Councilwoman Adams’ passion in issues around water resource management and long-term resiliency. I do like to highlight that Colorado’s urban water usage is only
~7% of our state’s demand
and our focus there needs to be in proportion to the city’s main climate and resiliency goals.

One place I want to highlight from Councilwoman Adams' campaigning is the need for stronger police oversight and a reduction in tools of mass surveillance, and policies that harm our civil liberties, particularly for minoritized populations. Boulder continues to
weaken its police oversight
year over year and I don’t see that pattern reversing without people willing to lead on the issue.
I will be ranking Taishya Adams second on my ballot.
Thoughts on other Candidates
Jameson “Jamo” Goldstein

I appreciate that Jamo is running in the election this year. As I have been a huge proponent of moving Boulder’s municipal elections to even years and paying our council-people a reasonable wage (I was a co-lead on campaigns for these issues), it’s encouraging to see a 21-year-old student at CU running on the ballot.

While I don’t think Jamo is running a particularly progressive campaign (in opposing Boulder’s deferred maintenance plan, and previously having a position on his website that said car “parking is a human right”), I do appreciate his positions on removing Flock cameras and improving the city’s transportation with its Core Arterial Network (CAN) implementation.

I hope CU students continue to run for city council (which I think would be a more sensible choice than mayor) and use such campaigns to highlight city issues that directly affect students. While students may be here for only four or five years on average, the issues affecting students are ever-present. Although it’s a common belief in some circles (Boulder’s Nextdoor) that students greatly affect city elections, the turnout rate from CU students in off-years has typically ranged in the 15-25% (with
2025 as the last reference

While students registered within Boulder are still a relatively small part of Boulder’s electorate, I do expect that we’ll have the largest change in the number of students voting in a municipal election since 1971. That year, the US ratified the 26th amendment and voters aged 18, 19, and 20 were able to vote for the first time. That election saw the first Black resident elected to Boulder City Council (Penfield Tate, who was selected as mayor), four incumbents unseated, and the city passed a charter amendment to limit building heights to 55 feet (
Boulder County History: ’71 election unseated incumbents, brought height limit - Boulder Daily Camera
Do I expect the 2026 election to be so disruptive to the status quo? No. But it’s certainly going to be different.
Aquiles La Grave

Aquiles La Grave grew up in Boulder. While he has not been directly involved in city politics before last year, I had a number of questions about his candidacy and had wanted to share what I have researched.

In 2012, La Grave was living in Louisville, Colorado and became involved in a local housing issue. La Grave was a founding member of the Louisville Citizens’ Action Council, which formed the year prior to oppose a planned set of apartments at the Safeway on South Boulder Road. In the article “
The deal is dead: Louisville evaluates its prospects at Safeway site
” in June 2012:

Aquiles La Grave, a 10-year resident whose home is just north of the Village Square shopping center, said he and his neighbors want more than anything to see something replace the 55,000-square-foot building that housed the Safeway for 30 years. But it has to be the right project.

“We want to make sure that what goes in there doesn’t degrade our quality of life,” he said. “An empty Safeway is not impacting our neighborhood in any way except aesthetically — so we can be patient.”

The opposition delayed re-development of the empty shopping center by 12+ months, reducing the amount of housing proposed by nearly 40%. Through the process, the plan also included an Alfalfa’s grocery store at the reduced-housing site (
Developer, Alfalfa’s president present Safeway redevelopment plan

Faun Ellwood-Digel, who has lived in Louisville for 15 years, said she would prefer to see an even more scaled back development of the apartment complex — fewer than 100 units — but bringing in the grocer makes for a “reasonable tradeoff” for upwards of 120 units.
As you may know, Alfalfa’s closed that location and
its business entirely in 2021
. Unfortunately, neither the reduced housing nor the closure of the grocery store were good outcomes from Louisville.

You might be saying, that was almost fifteen years ago — how is that story relevant to what’s happening in Boulder today? I have been disturbed by a continued pattern I see of opposition to housing and development in Boulder. Here is a Facebook post from La Grave in August:

children.text: For reference, Boulder’s Alpine Balsam project will have both a consolidation of city office buildings as well as significant housing (144 city subsidized affordable units — which as far as I understand would be the largest single development of affordable units yet in Boulder). In my opinion, La Grave’s accusations that that city may have misused affordable housing funds on this site are misinformation that undermine confidence in the city’s ability to complete the buildout of the city offices as well as provide this housing that Boulder certainly needs.
In September, I saw another concerning post from La Grave on Nextdoor. I referenced earlier that the Boulder Valley School District
put out a plan

in late August to potentially close several schools in the Boulder area due to declining enrollment. La Grave’s “just asking questions” post on Nextdoor insinuates that the school district may be intending to close Flatirons elementary such that it could build residential housing on a school property that would not be subject to local zoning.

A post like this is simply intended to scare voters on Nextdoor who have NIMBY-ish tendencies and would certainly find such a plan concerning — at a time when everyone is rightly concerned about school closings. However, BVSD rarely divests in school properties (the last time was
Washington School in 2009
which was sold to a co-housing developer) and such discussion was not part of any school closure plan.

children.text: Additionally, in the past year, La Grave has been involved with redevelopment of the Boulder County North Broadway Complex attached to the Iris Ballfields. La Grave has been working with the committee “Save Iris Ballfields” in order to have the ballfields remain as part of any redevelopment proposal there.
Boulder Reporting Lab documented the
Boulder County site sales proposals in 2025
. Here are the top two of five proposals:
1333 Iris Avenue Acquisition LLC
(John Kirkland)
Offer:
$43 million
Use:
Housing, including an estimated 200+ affordable units
Would it preserve the ball fields?:
No
The Academy
endorsed by the North Boulder Little League
Offer:
$26 million
Use:
Senior living community
Would it preserve the ball fields?:
Yes
So, there are a number of factors here at play:
How much money Boulder County will make from the sale of property, which directly affects county budgets
How much housing will be built (and its relative affordability) on a site that supports lots of housing on a primary transit corridor
Whether or not the ballfields would be preserved (which many in the community find to be a community value)

Boulder County ultimately chose La Grave’s preferred proposal from The Academy, a senior housing developer. The opportunity costs for that move were a $17 million reduction from the county budget, and a greatly reduced amount and type of housing built at the site, while keeping the Iris Ballfields. Were there potentially other options that raised more money for Boulder County, built more housing, and still preserved the ballfields? Yes, quite possibly — but these were the options presented.

Whether or not you think that the City and County of Boulder should have preserved the Iris Ballfields (which certainly do have a community benefit), I have a lot of trouble with the consistent pattern in La Grave’s activism and campaign messaging. He’s running on a campaign of governance and financial stewardship, taking opportunities to lambast the city and staff over housing projects at Alpine Balsam and vehemently fighting against the City of Boulder 2K measure that would fund deferred maintenance on city buildings.

At the same time, Boulder still has significant affordable housing needs and budget challenges that I don’t believe La Grave’s approaches are suited to fixing. I believe his inexperience at dealing with the real issues that the city faces (and particularly that he is running for mayor rather than for city council) are not going to help Boulder emerge strongly through this next chapter.
Lastly, La Grave recently made a post on October 2nd in which he undermines the City of Boulder’s excellent
public matching funds program

for elections in order to make an attack on the current mayor. I’m a strong believer in public matching funds as a way to help level the playing field for candidates with less financial means, and I also used matching funds when I ran for Boulder City Council in 2017.
Per the City of Boulder, the
limitations are as follows

, in order to maintain integrity in our elections and not have them overrun by massive spending imbalances and corporate funding. It also aligns the city and candidates with good incentives for campaigns:
To accept only contributions from a natural person (no LLCs, non-profits, corporations, etc.).

To limit her or his expenditures to a predetermined expenditure limit. Candidate expenditures, expenditures by the candidate’s official campaign committee, and any coordinated expenditures with other persons all apply toward this expenditure limit. [Note: in 2026, this limit is approximately $25,000]
To contribute to her/his campaign no more than 20% of the expenditure limit from her/his own personal wealth. (This includes both monetary and non-monetary contributions.)
To return at least 50% of any unexpended funds to the city, but not more than the matching funds received.

In return, candidates also have a strong incentive to take matching funds: the city offers a one-to-one match for each donation. As donations are limited to $100 per person, campaigns with lots of grassroots support can definitely be competitive even if they don’t have wealthy donors.

children.text: I have a number of issues with this framing and such disingenuous attacks make it very difficult to trust a candidate.
Asserting that a candidate “took” money from taxpayers by using a city-sponsored system is a bad-faith attack on a candidate and our city.
The vast majority of candidates (and especially winning candidates) take public matching funds. The last significant candidate not to take matching funds was Bob Yates running for Mayor in 2023: (
In the race for Boulder mayor, Councilmember Bob Yates has raised more money than all his rivals combined
— Boulder Reporting Lab

A significant limitation in taking matching funds is that the candidate cannot self-fund their own campaign more than a few thousand dollars. However, La Grave does not have that limitation, and would be free to spend tens of thousands of dollars on his own campaign in the last few weeks. Personally financing a campaign can have a significant effect on the outcome, as a CU Regent candidate
spent over $100,000 of his own money
in the June 2026 Primary, much of that in the final weeks of the race.
Also, in not taking matching funds, a candidate like La Grave is not bound by the strict ~$25k expenditure limit. Notably, La Grave has already donated $10,000 to the
Big Tent BoCo
[Five Commissioners] initiative in 2026, so it is not unreasonable that he may consider additionally self-funding his campaign. When he posted above the graphic to Reddit,
multiple
people
asked if he would abide by the spending limit that candidates with matching funds agree to. La Grave did not answer those questions while answering several others in the thread.

abrupt resignation from Mark Wallach
in August after a vote on the future of the Boulder airport. A total of three incumbents are running for five seats, leading to a strong field of candidates overall.

These five candidates bring a strong mix of progressive values, experience on city council, as well as in our school district, while also bringing a new energy and vision to move the city forward (two incumbents and three new members). Here’s a bit more about each:
Ryan Schuchard

Housing, Capital, and the Contradictions of Progressive Urbanism in Boulder, Colorado

.” We also worked together directly on the campaign to move Boulder’s municipal elections to even years (which she chaired), and I’ve been glad to see Jill support a number of progressive causes over the years.

Tina is an incumbent with significant experience as a former president of the BVSD board and now serving on council for the past three years. Her openness to housing and zoning changes, as well as her thoughtfulness on the

and

have been significant. Tina always approaches our city’s problems with an open mind and then works hard to find the best path forward.

While I wouldn’t label Tara as a progressive based on a number of her positions and voting record (particularly on topics around policing, minimum wage, and related issues), I do think Tara has made good contributions on city council to support more housing and being an influential voice for improving transportation in Boulder. Amendment 82 (CONSTITUTIONAL):
NO / AGAINST

Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution creating new law granting the right for consumers to purchase natural gas for cooking or heating in homes or businesses and for distributors and utilities to sell natural gas to consumers?
Who put the measure on the ballot?
Amendment 82 was placed on the ballot through a citizen initiative backed by operatives of
Advance Colorado
, a right-wing group supporting numerous measures on Colorado’s 2026 ballot.
Short Description:

Establishes a constitutional right for consumers to purchase natural gas for use in homes and businesses and a right for producers, distributors, and utilities to sell natural gas, subject to the measure's terms.
Analysis and Commentary:
Oppose. Amendment 82 was placed on the ballot through a citizen initiative backed by operatives of
Advance Colorado
, a right-wing group supporting numerous measures on Colorado’s 2026 ballot.

Amendment 82 is simple enough: putting a requirement that Coloradans use a particular energy source into the state constitution. Why should we require the use of any fuel, material, or otherwise in the state constitution? We shouldn’t.

Currently, natural gas is and will continue to be freely available in Colorado to consumers for purchase and businesses to sell. There’s no imminent state law, or city/county code aiming to threaten that. However, we do have a number of forward-thinking plans addressing how we might use natural gas and other fossil fuels in the future. In late 2025, the Colorado Public Utilities Commission approved such a plan:

The Public Utilities Commission approved a “Clean Heat Plan” that calls for the state’s natural gas utilities to cut emissions from delivering and burning natural gas by 41% in the next 10 years, and all natural gas emissions entirely by 2050. We talked to state regulators, clean energy officials and advocates, and consumer groups for answers to your most urgent questions.
Colorado plans to phase out natural gas heating in homes, prompting many reader questions. We have answers.
— Colorado Sun

The reality is that with new advances in appliances, home batteries, and electrical power generation, moving to all-electric residential and commercial buildings will be cheaper, safer, and with fewer emissions. The plan recognizes that the state will need significant investment and subsidies to meet the goal. Even so, the 2050 target date does not propose any additional regulation on propane tanks or other natural gas uses. Within this plan, a full transition will take decades, which is why it’s important not to undermine such efforts by putting a mandate to use natural gas in the state constitution.
Living in Boulder, Amendment 82 would overturn local ordinances that the city has implemented to speed the transition. Since December 2024, building code updates now
require all-electric construction

for new or substantially-retrofitted buildings. Cities need to move ahead of the curve on new construction because a building built today may last 50 or 100 years with energy infrastructure investments that will be obsolete by that time. Even if you are a fierce defender of natural gas usage, the ordinance allowed reasonable exceptions for “commercial buildings, including those with commercial kitchens and laboratories,” according to Boulder Reporting Lab.

Ultimately, there’s no good reason to require the use of natural gas in the state constitution. Our state and local governments need to be vigilant in moving ahead on an energy transition, and ensuring that every person and family in Colorado has the means to economically transition our energy supply. If Amendment 82 were to pass, that means we will undermine our own energy goals, add sunken infrastructure costs over the next several decades, and ultimately have to undo a measure that would be a significant mistake.

NO / AGAINST

Shall there be an amendment to the Colorado Constitution concerning ballot question language, and, in connection therewith, requiring all state and local ballot questions to be written in plain language and at no more than an 8th grade reading level and prohibiting a state statute from requiring language that conflicts with these requirements in ballot questions for citizen-initiated measures?
Who put the measure on the ballot?

Oppose. Amendment 85 was placed on the ballot through a citizen initiative backed by operatives of
Advance Colorado
, a right-wing group supporting numerous measures on Colorado’s 2026 ballot.

Amendment 85 is the most insidious measure on Colorado’s 2026 ballot. Claiming to make the ballot accessible to voters at an eighth-grade level, the constitutional amendment would give voters less information and make measures subject to even more legal scrutiny before being placed on the ballot.
I’m going to cite the Colorado Blue Book which states a very plain argument for why the constitutional amendment is a problem: “This measure puts vague and undefined language in the constitution.”

This measure is unnecessary as state law already provides ample guidance for the preparation of ballot titles in plain language. Ballot titles must convey important information to voters about complex policies. This measure creates a constitutional standard with no guidance about how its requirements are different from current law. This could lead to more challenges of initiative ballot titles, impacting the initiative process.
Amendment 85, Colorado Blue Book
So what is the intent of this constitutional amendment, really?
I don’t normally agree with conservative commentator Krista Kafer on much of anything, but she had a solid opinion piece on Amendment 85 / Initiative 234, stating:

Initiative 234 may seem simple but the intent of this measure isn’t so plain. Colorado law already requires ballot measures be written in understandable language accessible to the “widest possible audience.” Could this ballot initiative be about power rather than accessibility?
If the constitutional amendment passes, it will be more difficult to render fiscal and taxation impact information into middle school reading material.
Information empowers voters and Initiative 234 strips away vital knowledge (Opinion)

HB21-1321 - Voter Transparency In Ballot Measures

which “requires the fiscal impact statement and ballot information booklet entry for the following types of initiated measures to include a description of the measure's likely effect on the 3 largest areas of program expenditure of the state.”
Such laws may have to be amended or weakened with the passage of Amendment 85.

Speaking from personal experience as a political organizer and professional campaigner, and having been involved in writing several local ballot questions: ballot measures which have clear and simple language are much more likely to pass than measures that are complex and confusing. Our state constitution and election laws already reflect that, and I am voting against Amendment 85.

In 2018, Colorado voters passed Amendments X and Y, which set up requirements for the state’s redistricting of US House seats and all state legislature seats, requiring an independent / cross-partisan commission. That process takes place every ten years after the U.S. Decennial Census.

I supported those measures in 2018, and still believe the process is a good one for Colorado, particularly for our state legislature. Gerrymandering of representative seats leads to terrible power dynamics, bad incentives for legislators and districts, and is bad for democracy.

However, Republicans nationally, and conservatives on the United States Supreme Court, have broken that contract with voters at the federal level, which is why Colorado needs flexibility to manage its redistricting system. Look no further than mid-cycle redistricting efforts by Republican-led states of Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas all attempted or enacted efforts to
increase Republican gerrymanders
mid-cycle between 2024 and 2026. That’s on top of the conservative Supreme Court completing their
dismantling of the Voting Rights Act

which has continued to enable more partisan and racial gerrymanders. In many ways, Colorado passing Amendment Y for congressional redistricting was preemptive disarmament in a war that Republicans intend to wage until the end.
Conversely in 2021, US House Democrats passed
HR1: For the People Act of 2021

. Among other national voter protections, the bill would have required that “states to establish independent redistricting commissions to carry out congressional redistricting,” like the system that Colorado has independently approved. However, rather famously, the bill was

Proposition 137 is a well-intentioned measure, with some useful investments in state outdoors priorities. However, I do not support the measure because its passage would exempt the funding from TABOR, which places this funding above priorities like health care, education, and human services.
Here’s where Proposition 137 would do, according to the Colorado Blue Book:

47.5% - Great Outdoors Colorado (GOCO). About $83.1 million would be dedicated to GOCO, an organization established in the state constitution that funds parks, trails, and wildlife projects through grants to local governments, the state, and other conservation efforts. GOCO is funded by the state lottery, amounting to about $90 million annually, and currently receives no state funding from taxes.

47.5% - Wildfire risk mitigation, forest management, and watershed restoration projects. About $83.1 million would be dedicated to these efforts per year. In budget year 2027-28, a one-time investment of $10.0 million would be made out of the total funding available to pay for damages that may arise from the use of prescribed fires. These wildfire risk mitigation and forest management efforts currently receive about $16.4 million annually from the state, which is largely awarded through grants from state agencies for fuels reduction in forests and other risk mitigation projects near developed areas. Watershed restoration projects and water projects reducing risk of post-wildfire floods currently receive about $5 million annually from the state.

5% - Outdoor recreation, economic development, and equity programs. The remaining revenue, about $8.7 million, would be dedicated to outdoor recreation and equity programs funded through the Colorado Office of Economic Development and International Trade and Colorado Parks and Wildlife. These programs currently receive about $800,000 from the state annually. The funding is used to support outdoor industry business advancement and outdoor recreation planning for rural communities, and to provide grants to organizations and projects improving access and representation for youth and their families in the Colorado outdoors.
Proposition 137, Colorado Blue Book

According to the Colorado Blue Book, “The measure will decrease the amount refunded to taxpayers in years when state revenue is over the TABOR limit,” which is the expected outcome of dedicated spending. However, that same dedicated funding mechanism will negatively affect spending we have dedicated for general fund priorities like healthcare, childcare, and education. “In years where state revenue is below the TABOR limit, the measure does not impact TABOR refunds, but it may reduce the amount of money available for other general budget priorities.”
The effect would be compounded with if we pass Proposition NN:

Proposition NN allows the state to keep and spend revenue that would otherwise be refunded to taxpayers under TABOR, up to a newly established limit. Because Proposition 137 reduces revenue subject to the constitutional revenue limit,
Proposition 137 will reduce the amount of money the state actually keeps and spends under Proposition NN, if both measures pass.
Proposition 137, Colorado Blue Book
A few groups that might be otherwise supportive (like the Colorado Democratic Party and Boulder Progressives), are opposed to the measure because of the spending effects. Per the Colorado Sun:
No committee has formed to oppose Proposition 137, but the League of Women Voters
opposes the ballot measure
, saying the “permanent transfer” of funds from the “perpetually short” state general fund, “
does not allow for legislative judgment.

Boulder County Ballot Question 200: NO POSITION
Shall the membership of the Boulder County Board of Commissioners be increased from a three member board to a five member board?
Who put the measure on the ballot?

Short Description:

Expands the Boulder County Board of County Commissioners from three members to five. Organizers submitted 18,422 signatures; the Clerk issued a statement of sufficiency on August 5, and the commissioners certified the measure on August 25.
Analysis and Commentary:

I ultimately decided to go with “No position” on Measure 200, which is a first in the 10+ year history of Boulder Colorado Voter Guide. I have struggled with deciding my vote for many months, and tried to capture all of my thinking here. First I’ll address what I think are the most compelling reasons I found to vote No, and several compelling reasons for a Yes vote.
Compelling reasons to vote No:

Boulder County’s commissioners can move more quickly with only three commissioners. The roles have traditionally been less a legislative body and more managerial. Traditionally, commissioners had a staff and management component. Only since 2020 has the county had a county administrator (similar to a city manager) that staff reported to (and that
person has recently resigned

While many proponents state that having five commissioners as increasing accountability, I’m not sure how that argument makes sense. By nature, increasing the number of people making a decision would decrease the amount of accountability any one person has in the decision. Regardless of whether we move to a district model (which I oppose) or a three-district, two at-large model, I don’t see how you can argue it makes the system more accountable.

Moving to a five-district model would be a truly bad outcome. While the current model of three commissioners, all at-large, also has some negative aspects, having five districts would divide up the county awkwardly (cutting up three population areas into five parts) and removes the incentive to work together as a whole to solve the county’s challenges, and promotes the incentive to do what’s best for one’s own district. I write more about this on Boulder County Measure 201.

There’s also a cost to increasing the number of commissioners. While not my favorite argument, the reality is that adding two commissioners will increase the county budget by $400-500k, while at the same time Boulder County’s 2027 budget already has significant cuts due to decreased revenues,
eliminating 36 positions which includes 10-15 layoffs
. The increased cost might be justified if convincingly showed a tangible improvement in governance but I’m not sure that it will.
I’ve spoken with two people I respect greatly, former County Commissioners Will Toor and Elise Jones, who oppose the change, and outlined eight solid arguments against the change as well:
Five current and former Boulder County commissioners: Don’t expand the commission to five seats
— Boulder Reporting Lab
I don’t particularly trust the group
Big Tent BoCo

, which put the measure on the ballot. The group leans moderate to conservative as a whole, and I presume that the intention is to try to expand their influence in Boulder County. The group has accepted $20,000 from Boulder conservative / Trump voter Dan Caruso, as well as $10,000 from Aquiles La Grave, and $10,000 from Kent Thiry, one of the primary funders behind the narrowly-defeated 2024 ballot measure
Proposition 131

which would have drastically changed Colorado’s primary and general election system. I like to judge measures based on their merits but like most everything on Colorado’s 2026 ballot, you also have to consider the source.
Now, the Yes arguments that I find compelling:

How we elect county commissioners has often been not well-contested in the past fifteen years. Because Boulder is a heavily Democratic county, the only potential competitive races are in the Democratic Primary. We had one closely contested race in 2020, one in 2022, and a fairly uneven race in 2012. I do think more races would be contested and open if we moved to five commissioners, but likely more so with the 3-district / 2 at large rather than the five district system.

The current commissioners don’t seem to discuss policy and work together well due to open meetings laws and requirements for transparency. A discussion between two commissioners about a policy item is problematic when that is also a quorum of the board. It’s possible that having five commissioners might improve communication.

Right now, a commission of three leads to a lot of bad incentives. I was having a conversation with my fellow Boulder Progressives board member Adrian Fine — Adrian was previously the Mayor of Palo Alto before moving to Boulder. He has a few insights from his time as an elected official that I’d like to share:

“With 3: if you're on the losing side, the majority knows that and the dynamics become multiple against singular. With a 4th or 5th vote, the majority cannot just be against 1 person; they have to earn/please/placate at least one more. So the extra vote prevents railroading behavior.”

If you're trying to assemble a winning coalition, it means it cannot just be you and one other, you are going to have to get a 3rd opinion. Your argument for or against something cannot just be tailored to the one, only other person that matters.
“And it's not just the elected officials. Staff has the exact same incentive; ‘oh we know the commission is split? let's build X report to persuade the middle’”
Currently, it may be more difficult to meet with the commissioners because there are few of them or work may be held up by the absence of a single commissioner.

While not a great argument for a systemic change, a lot of people have significant grievances and mistrust with the current set of commissioners. Some people like the idea of a fresh start with a larger group. However, that’s somewhat moot because two of the commissioners will be term-limited in 2028.

I tend to be pretty open-minded, and have been grappling with this commissioner question for the past 8+ months. I still don’t have a much better direction than when I first started thinking about the issue. I also find myself thinking about the City of Boulder’s move to directly elect its mayor in 2020 (with the first election in 2023). The measure was popular, I supported it with mixed feelings, and it
passed with 78.14%

of the vote. I understand the appeal of voting for mayor plus four council people compared to voting for five council people, but I am not sure it necessarily made our governance any better. We do not have a strong mayor system, and decisions are still made by five votes on council and working with the city manager to implement that vision.
The commissioners ballot measure certainly has trade-offs. I’m not certain that the trade-offs with five commissioners are better than the trade-offs of the current system. We will see what happens.

Commissioners in five districts have incentives to be insular in their thinking — putting the needs of the people in their own district above the county’s needs as a whole.

Single-winner districts means that the county may miss out on the service of good candidates because there can only be one winner per district. It also means that in some cycles, there may be a lack of good candidates in a particular district. These problems are mitigated by having both larger districts and at-large seats.

Should three district-elected commissioners be joined by two commissioners elected countywide?
Here are my arguments for three districts, and two at-large:

For someone like me who is skeptical of the benefits of five commissioners, moving to three districts, two at-large would be a smaller change from the current system. The same existing districts could be used for the new system, which are relatively aligned with Boulder County’s population centers

Right now all Boulder County residents get to vote on all commissioners, three in total. In the five district system, each person would only get to vote on one commissioner, which is a significant downgrade in influence. In Option B, people would still get to vote for three of five commissioners — one in their own district, and two at-large

In having both districts and at-large, potential candidates can weigh which is a better fit for themselves based on their geographical location, experience in elected office, and relationships across the county.

When two strong candidates live in the same district, one may choose to run at-large. That can be a benefit to the county to have both as options for election. As I have mentioned, even with five districts, Boulder or Longmont would very likely have two people representing each city because these population centers would be split. With an at-large system, you might still get two commissioners from the same city, but they won’t be strictly eligible in one district based on a district barrier.

Analysis and Commentary:
Support. City of Boulder Issue 2J was placed on the ballot by the Boulder City Council through
Ordinance 8759
Boulder’s vacancy tax came onto the ballot after several years of work by city councilpeople and community organizing. The main community concerns that raised the idea of a vacancy tax are:
Boulder is a town with significant wealth and residents that own homes in Boulder that are used as second homes, and often unoccupied

Unoccupied homes do not contribute to the local economy through sales taxes, nor provide people to work in the local economy, and kids to attend our schools. A tax is meant to reduce that behavior and encourage owners that are present in the community. Otherwise, the tax goes to support city budgets for public services that the city must provide regardless.

With Boulder now hosting the Sundance Film Festival starting in 2027, people in the community have felt additional urgency to address homes that are largely unoccupied and simply treated as luxury investments, which may increase with Sundance’s arrival.

I appreciated researching the effectiveness of residential vacancy taxes, as I’m somewhat skeptical about whether the new tax would change behavior or raise significant money for the city’s general fund. Some research in Vancouver showed a measurable but small effect:

It’s difficult to attribute increases in rental units and declines in vacancy to this tax alone, but the city’s calculations show a slight uptick in available housing units, particularly among condominiums and single-family homes. Despite widespread adoption of these regulatory tools to combat housing availability, residents in Vancouver continue to worry about affordability and neighborhood stability caused by vacancies.
Local Vacancy Taxes: A Tool but Not a Panacea
— Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy

One difference that has concerned me is that the tax as structured is only $4,000 per year, which doesn’t make sense to me compared to rate more variables based on property value (i.e. Vancouver’s 3%). So the effect on a condo worth $400,000 is much greater than the effect on a detached home with $2,000,000. I’m certainly concerned that overhead and management of the tax may make the exercise not very economically efficient.

The City of Boulder projects that the tax will raise $6,000,000 annually, based on a projected 1,500 units subject to the tax at $4,000 per unit. It’s difficult to determine how likely the unit and total revenue estimates are to be correct.

Part of the reason for that uncertainty is because a second ordinance will be needed to implement the tax once voters approve it. Details such as what reasonable exemptions are allowed (i.e. remodels, in the process of trying to rent or sell a property, etc) will need to be implemented next year, and may affect overall taxation rates.

Overall, I would like to see the tax work and effectively raise money or change behavior. I hope that the council is willing to make adjustments or enable future ballot measures to get the details right if needed.

Analysis and Commentary:
Support. City of Boulder Issue 2K was placed on the ballot by the Boulder City Council through
Ordinance 8758

Boulder Issue 2K is the most controversial local issue on Boulder's 2026 ballot. What’s not controversial is that a number of city-owned buildings are in disrepair or near the end of their usable life. The controversial part is what do we pay to address the deferred maintenance and when?

I strongly support Issue 2K. I’ll outline the basics and how I got there. I also want to mention how our Boulder City Council, with an 8-0 vote, supported putting the bond on the ballot. Setting election politics aside, that’s a strong show of support from every council person across ideological lines.
Ballot Issue 2K Overview:
What does the bond do and why do we need it?
What if we made the bond smaller?
What if we vote on this again in 2027 or 2028?
What happens if we don’t address the problem?
Is the cost for individuals and businesses too high?
What does the bond do and why do we need it?
Boulder has a
Facilities Master Plan
which “provides a strategic direction for 75 buildings, with over 1.8 M square feet of space and a current replacement value of over $550M.” The Boulder Issue 2K
Recreation and Safety Bond
proposes “$400 million to pay for specific infrastructure projects” along with estimated costs and justifications for why buildings need replacement or serious remodeling.
South Boulder Recreation Center - $65,000,000
North Boulder Recreation Center - $72,000,000
West Age Well Center - (costs part of North Boulder Recreation Center)
Fire Station No. 1 - $5,000,000
Fire Station No. 5 - $2,000,000
Public Safety Center and 911 Dispatch - $170,000,000 (depends on selected location; this cost includes likely site infrastructure and construction of secure parking)
Municipal Services Center - $100,000,000
Penfield Tate II Municipal Building - $30,000,000
An important detail is that the city may stagger reconstruction burden and would not immediately bond for the full cost:

If the city bonded for the full $400 million, the owner of a property that is worth $1 million would pay an additional $400 a year in property taxes for 20 years. If the city bonds for less or staggers projects, the property tax impact would be less. It is likely that the city would sequence how much it borrows, so the full increase is unlikely to occur for a couple of years.

The other factor at play is: the city is passing a measure for the full bonding costs of facilities. However, because TABOR requires voters to pass such authorization, the city has an incentive to estimate the highest cost so that they don’t have to ask voters again for additional money. That’s not to say that voters should *expect* a lower total cost, but the city can and should take opportunities for cost reductions and alternatives where possible.

A good example is a recent proposal relayed from Boulder City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde. On September 24th, she emailed the Boulder City Council Hotline with updated information on the public safety building:

We have a late breaking opportunity to potentially lease and/or purchase an existing building in another location in the city that has the footprint needed to house PD operations. The potential cost of this acquisition and renovation would significantly reduce the costs needed to provide a future location for our police department’s future needs.

A number of people in progressive circles (including me) are not thrilled with Issue 2K’s allocation of funds, that roughly 42% of the bond funding would go to a new police station (as police operating revenue is approximately 10% of
Boulder’s proposed 2027 budget

). While such an alternative plan is still preliminary, the city could build a lot of good will by reducing the police station cost to balance spending over various needs. A new location may last Boulder another 50-75+ years:

The Public Safety Building, 1805 33rd Street, was built in 1968. It was the home of the Mountain Bell telephone company before the city purchased it in 1988 for about $2.7 million, according to county property records, and the police moved their operations there around 1989.
Boulder says it needs $170M to replace a failing Public Safety Building. Here’s why.
— Boulder Daily Camera

I won’t go over every project individually, but a number of the individual projects seem popular with the community: updating or reconstructing the South Boulder and North Boulder recreation centers, repairing and renovating fire stations 1 and 5, and creating a new / updated space for the West Age Well Center to continue support for Boulder’s aging demographics.

It’s also important to note that passing the bond does not simply allow each project to go forward without further discussion. Every major item will come back to Boulder City Council for public input and process, which is exactly what’s needed in order to make sure the city is delivering the right implementation of these projects.
What if we made the bond smaller?

Some people have criticized Boulder’s deferred maintenance bond as “too large.” The reality is that no one wants to pay for deferred maintenance. It’s not fun, it’s not sexy — it’s not anything other than a debt that in Boulder’s case, which hasn’t been paid or saved for in decades.

The City of Boulder polled on the measure in June and found the public split on whether to support the bond. However, a notable finding: a reduced bond paying for a smaller set of higher-priority buildings actually polled
worse
than the larger bond.

children.alt: City of Boulder poll results on the Issue 2K Recreation and Safety Bond

children.text: The city has outlined project start timelines based on priority, so a reduced bond would target those projects first:

Work on the city’s Public Safety Building relocation would begin first. The city has identified this building as having the greatest number of repair needs. This project would cost the most and would take the longest to complete. By starting soon, the city could limit cost increases that come with delays. If the city can add staff, it would be able to start planning other projects at the same time. The goal would be to finish all the projects within 10 years.
Recreation and Safety Bond
— City of Boulder
So, if you are asking for a smaller bond, it’s going to be the public safety building first, and other priorities second. You might understand why that option would poll worse.

Even if the council brought back a smaller bond in 2027 and 2028, and miraculously passed it (which I’m skeptical about), then you have the problem of lumping less-popular projects together to pass future bond measures. That’s a bad outcome for the city.
In an
opinion piece

from former Boulder Representative and City council person KC Becker asking for more process on the bond, I wanted to highlight a comment from former Boulder City Councilperson Bob Yates. He later made a more inflammatory comment on Boulder Nextdoor that I think is instructive:

children.alt: Boulder 2011 bond process notes on deferred maintenance from the Issue 2K discussion

children.text: I have a couple issues with this framing. Part of it is what I already said — TABOR will give the incentives for the city to pass popular measures, when not every need the city has is popular. It’s notable that Bob said in his
latest newsletter
, “All I can say is, thank goodness for TABOR” when lodging his opposition to most taxes on this year’s ballot.

Secondly, Bob says that the committee “winnowed the staff’s wish list down from $700 million to $49 million” back in 2011. As an astute, longtime observer of Boulder politics mentioned to me: "Hmm, did going from $700M to $49M involve deferring any maintenance? I'll wait..."

My Boulder Progressives colleague Brian Keegan pointed me to his additional research on previous deferred maintenance conversations. Here is more context in decisions by previous city councils and staff, with a relevant quote from the 2011 bond process:
“[Jane] Brautigam, the city manager, responded by saying that filling the entire gap now isn’t this government’s responsibility — but maintaining roads and buildings is.
“It is a funding gap that will exist in 2030,” she said. “It’s not our responsibility today to reduce a funding gap that’s going to occur 20 years from now.”
Boulder considers bonds, tax increases for capital improvements
— Boulder Daily Camera
Boulder’s problem with deferred maintenance is not new — the problem has been ignored and not paid for previously.
What if we vote on this again in 2027 or 2028?
If Boulder Issue 2K does not pass, and if Boulder comes up with a saleable smaller measure, what are the prospects of its passage in 2027 or 2028?
My professional opinion as part of my firm
Colorado Community Research

, which does ballot measure polling and political consulting, is that 2027 is dead in the water for a property tax measure. Off-year elections have a significant skew towards homeowners (closer to 75%, whereas city-wide is closer to 50%), as well as being more conservative. Given the currently mixed polling for an even-year electorate, trying to run a similar measure in an off-year would certainly fail. The only way to win such a measure is to make concessions to the loudest, most influential opponents of the measure currently (to gain their support), so that they are the deciders of how the city spends money, not the council or general public. That’s not a democratic outcome.

Running the measure in 2028 would delay the timeline another two years, and does increase uncertainty. The main risks are an economic downturn, which would again reduce the likelihood of passage. Another factor is that construction costs continue to rise faster than inflation, so projects would likely cost more by delaying them. Third, the city continues to pay for required and emergency deferred maintenance on these buildings out of the general fund, which continues to strain other parts of an already strained budget.
What happens if we don’t address the problem?

Beyond my concern that the city will continue spending a larger and larger part of the general fund on deferred maintenance, we are already seeing the effects of the City of Boulder’s decades-long negligence to deferred maintenance in what’s happening with our library budget.
The Boulder Public Library District formed after a 2022 vote, officially separating from the City of Boulder. As part of the formation, the City of Boulder has kept
ownership of the buildings

, but the library district has the responsibility to maintain them, including deferred maintenance. Now, due to a combination of state property tax cuts, lower than expected property tax values, and millions of dollars of deferred maintenance, the library district is now
cutting 20% of its staff

Additionally, the library buildings, which the district leases from the City of Boulder, are an average of 56 years old and require significant upkeep that has not been a major part of the district budget to date. Capital needs overall are expected to be higher in 2028 and 2029 because certain upgrades and necessary maintenance have been delayed and cannot be put off indefinitely. The current budget has little money allocated for facilities upkeep or future capital needs.
Boulder’s library district is cutting 20% of its staff. How did it get here?
— Boulder Reporting Lab

If Boulder voters need to understand how long-standing deferred maintenance can have a direct impact for ongoing operations and services, the challenges that the library district is working through is direct evidence.

What might that look like for Boulder? I’m not totally certain, but I can tell you that popular amenities like swimming pools and rec centers are more likely to be cut before funding for police officers. We’re already seeing a similar effect with
Boulder’s Spruce Pool

. While Boulder’s shortfalls in addressing public amenities like Spruce Pool are in operating costs rather than capital costs, if we do not address our capital funding shortfalls, they will continue to squeeze operations.
Is the cost for individuals and businesses too high?

I do think most of the pushback on the bond is about who pays and how much. I don’t take that lightly, and each voter will determine that for themselves. However, it’s fair to say that opposition is coming from
wealthier voters
, including Boulder conservative / Trump voter Dan Caruso.

As property taxes tend to be more progressive than not, I think it’s correct that voters owning more expensive properties should pay a higher share to address our infrastructure needs. It’s the correct position of the city to move toward property taxes to address these concerns rather than continuing to pay for long-term investments using regressive sales taxes. What will Boulder do this year? I’m looking forward to find out.

Short Description:

Amends the city charter so Boulder's debt limit is calculated as no more than three percent of the actual value of taxable property rather than assessed value. The city asserts this is consistent with how most municipalities and the state calculate debt limitation.
Analysis and Commentary:
Support. City of Boulder Issue 2M was placed on the ballot by the Boulder City Council through
Ordinance 8762

The City of Boulder is looking to update its charter to allow a more reasonable amount of debt to be authorized in order to pursue future projects. Note that this ballot measure does not authorize any new debt itself, which must be authorized through a specific ballot question.

City Debt Limitation Charter Amendment (Attachment D - Ord. 8762) This measure would amend Charter Sec. 97 so that debt limitation could be no more than the “actual value” (rather than the “assessed value” as currently written) of the taxable property within the city. This amendment would bring the city’s charter in line with all other Boulder County communities and state statute.
August 6th Agenda Packet, Boulder City Council
Boulder County has a useful
terminology web page
Actual Value is “That value determined by appropriate consideration of the cost approach, the market approach, and the income approach to appraisal.”

The assessed value is typically much lower, and determined by this formula: Assessed Value = Actual Value x Assessment Rate. The assessment rate is typically a fixed amount, i.e. 6.7% to determine what is taxable.
So in practice, the actual value is a significantly higher number and more reflective of a reasonable bonding amount — a maximum of 3% of the entire property value of all structures in the city.
Again, an important caveat — Measure 2M does not take on any new debt, and such debt must be authorized through other ballot measures.

The change to the city’s debt limitation would have no fiscal impact, but would allow the city to issue general obligation bonds above the current charter limitation of three percent of the assessed value of the taxable property within the city. Assessed value as of 2025 for Boulder is $5.0 billion. Based on the most recent assessed value, the city is limited to $150.7 million in general obligation debt.

What would Issue 7A do and why do we need it?
Issue 7A would institute a sales tax along the Front Range Passenger Rail district, which will serve as the primary funding source for passenger rail.

12 Front Range communities connected
190 total track miles from Fort Collins to Pueblo
2029 — Date that expanded service would begin
15 new CoCo stations (13 Daily and 2 Special Event Stations)

300-500 seats per train.
From an election perspective, state legislators made a smart choice to update the district boundaries before putting a measure to voters: “Under
, the district would be redrawn to a fraction of its current geographic size and shed about 40% of its population, shrinking to 2.6 million residents from 4.4 million,”

children.text: As far as service and number of trips, that is why Issue 7A is so important. Here is an explanation of the different phases of the project. children.text: As far as why we need better train infrastructure, here are my main interests:
Continue to provide better, non-highway transportation that connects Colorado’s greatest economic centers.

Invest in larger, people-mover type infrastructure. A heavy rail train moving 300-500 people at a time is a solid investment, significantly more than a single bus or light rail train in our urban areas.

Enabling and fostering the benefits of denser housing and business development. Expanding on existing hubs like Union Station and Boulder Junction, as well as giving incentives for more transit-oriented development, will be a boon for our cities.
Continuing to improve access all-electric transportation options, and reducing our reliance on automobiles for long-distance travel (“
Front Range Passenger Rail could deliver major transportation and environmental benefits
” — SWEEP)
Boulder has paid significant money for a train. Why should I support 7A?
As part of Phase 1 for Front Range Passenger Rail, Boulder is getting its train! That’s already paid for in combination with the Regional Transportation District (RTD):

The Front Range Passenger Rail District says it already has enough funds to create three round trips a day between Denver and Fort Collins in three years, with the route heading northwest to Boulder and Longmont on the way to Larimer County.

The $332 million limited phase cost would come from a state transportation innovation fund built up by various fees, and RTD money set aside for FasTracks rail lines north of Denver that were never built. The state and RTD would split the $30 million to $36 million annual operating costs for that phase.
Ballot Issue 7A: Front Range voters will weigh sales tax hike to pay for passenger train service
— Colorado Sun
However, the biggest risk to Front Range Passenger Rail’s initial implementation is that it will be
underwhelming

. Only running three trains per day, with minimal station investment, and not extending the entire length of the proposed system. Voting Yes on 7A will ensure the system is adequately funded over the long term and can bring additional revenue and matching grants to expand the system beyond the initial phase.
What happens if 7A fails?
If Issue 7A fails, we’re probably stuck with underwhelming train service, at best. The other issues is that it may jeopardize getting future grants to improve service, such as a
$66 million federal grant
in 2024 used to improve service between Broomfield and Westminster. It’s not clear what the path forward might be if Issue 7A fails.
How would 7A benefit Boulder and Denver specifically?

Here's a helpful map about where the train would intersect into Boulder. The station will be placed in Boulder Junction, which is a transit-first neighborhood in East Boulder that continues to improve year-over-year. The transit aspect of the neighborhood took a hit since COVID-19 caused the area to lose significant bus service in 2020, which has slowly been improving.

Boulder has pretty excellent transit service along the US 36 / Broadway corridor, but its service to East Boulder is lacking. Providing a long-term boost for residents and businesses in East Boulder could be a solid improvement to make Boulder transit less one-dimensional.

children.text: Denver is already well-served as the best transit hub in Colorado, but things can still get better. As an anchor to regional train service to Boulder, Fort Collins, Colorado Springs and Pueblo, Denver benefits from a strengthening region, all connected through Denver Union Station.

Colorado sports teams
